questions.question: A control task needs a stochastic policy over continuous torques, where taking argmax over actions is unsuitable. Which approach matches this need?
options: Enumerate the Bellman equation for every continuous action.
Use a tabular Q table and take the largest action value.
Parameterize the policy directly and sample actions from its distribution.
Use a deterministic argmax policy over every possible torque.
questions.explanation: A policy-gradient model parameterizes πθ(a|s) as a distribution and samples an action, rather than choosing argmax Q. A Gaussian policy can represent continuous torques; a tabular Q table or discrete softmax list does not cover that continuous action space.

questions.question: A softmax policy has probabilities [0.2, 0.5, 0.3], and the second action (index 1) was selected. What is the score gradient with respect to the three logits?
options: [0.2, 0.5, 0.3], the probability vector without adjustment.
[-0.5, -0.2, 0.3], probabilities reordered by action value.
[0.2, -0.5, 0.3], probabilities minus selected-action one-hot.
[-0.2, 0.5, -0.3], selected-action one-hot minus probabilities.
questions.explanation: For softmax logits, ∇logπ(a) = onehot(a) − π. The selected action is index 1, so [0,1,0]−[0.2,0.5,0.3]=[−0.2,0.5,−0.3]. The presented probabilities-minus-onehot option reverses every sign, while the raw probability vector omits the selected-action signal.

questions.question: A learned baseline uses only the state and not the sampled action. What effect does subtracting it from return have in REINFORCE?
options: It changes the expected gradient and increases variance.
It preserves the expected gradient while reducing variance.
It removes the policy distribution from the gradient update.
It converts the sampled return into a Bellman target.
questions.explanation: Subtracting b(s) leaves the expected policy gradient unchanged when the baseline does not depend on the sampled action, because Eπ[∇logπ(a|s)]=0. A learned value baseline can reduce return variance; an action-dependent baseline would not inherit this cancellation automatically.

questions.question: For the gradient at time t, why use reward-to-go rather than rewards received before time t?
options: Reward-to-go makes the update independent of the sampled action.
Past rewards determine the future policy, so they must receive larger discounts.
Past rewards add zero-mean noise because the current action cannot cause them.
Past rewards are always negative and would reverse the gradient.
questions.explanation: The action at time t cannot cause rewards that occurred before t, so those past rewards add zero-mean noise to its score-function estimate. Reward-to-go retains the future rewards that can depend on the action while lowering variance.

questions.question: A robot policy must output continuous joint torques. Which policy head named in the lesson fits this action space?
options: A one-hot policy that always picks the highest logit.
A value table that stores one entry per possible torque.
A softmax distribution over a fixed list of discrete moves.
A Gaussian policy whose mean and scale depend on the state.
questions.explanation: A Gaussian policy represents continuous actions by a state-dependent mean and scale, so it can sample torques from a continuous distribution. A softmax head assigns probabilities to a fixed discrete action list instead.

questions.question: Training drives the policy entropy near zero before it has explored useful actions. Which objective adjustment directly addresses this collapse?
options: Replace reward-to-go with the full episode return at every step.
Add a positive entropy bonus to encourage continued exploration.
Remove the baseline so returns have larger variance.
Increase the action count without changing the policy objective.
questions.explanation: Policy entropy measures how spread the action distribution remains; adding a positive βH term rewards preserving that spread during training. Removing the baseline may increase gradient variance, but it does not directly oppose premature concentration on one action.
